title: Any movement with a pain byproduct is a bad exercise (for you)
summary: Distinguishes good pain (pump, muscle burn) from joint/tendon pain and argues that any exercise causing the latter is a bad exercise for you. Recommends re-evaluating form, stance and style, then dropping the lift if pain persists; there are no must-do exercises for bodybuilders. Illustrated by his own ego-driven years on wrist curls, standing skull crushers and a failed sumo experiment.

claims.claim: There are two types of pain in lifting: the pain of a pump or a muscle being properly targeted, and the pain of a ligament, tendon or something not being right; with some experience the difference is easy to tell.
People who avoid hard work like high reps because they're painful won't amount to anything anyway; his advice is for people who push themselves.
If an exercise gives you joint pain, stop doing it; people keep going because of ego or outside pressure, but only your body matters.
When you feel wrist, elbow, shoulder, knee or lower back pain, first examine your form; if a form change removes the pain, continue the exercise.
If fixing form doesn't remove the pain, try switching stance or style; many people who can't deadlift conventional feel great pulling sumo and get extra lower back work elsewhere.
Don't think you must do a lift just because it's one of the big three; push-ups agree with more people than the bench press, which was chosen for powerlifting for other reasons.
There is no such thing as a must-do exercise for bodybuilders: do whatever targets the right muscle; only powerlifters must abide by competition lifts.
No exercise should have a pain byproduct; waking up with a sore lower back after deadlifts means you're deadlifting wrong or using a variation that doesn't fit your body type.
Tissue damage stays when muscle mass is lost later in life, so painful training now will cause serious problems when you're older.
Do what works for you no matter how stupid it looks to others.
He is very stubborn and kept painful exercises for years because he believed they were the best; he only recently dropped wrist curls after years because they destroyed his wrists.
He dropped standing skull crushers, done because he could use 150-160 lbs, versus about 90 lbs for 4x10 on lying skull crushers; the standing version was hurting his wrists.
Lying skull crushers with ego aside and a full stretch give better gains and healthy tendons than heavier but painful variants.
Pain shouldn't be part of your training.
If it hurts: stop and re-evaluate; if it still hurts, re-evaluate again and do your research; if you've tried everything, move on to another exercise.
Even though he loves conventional deadlifts, he rejects the dogma that you're a coward if you don't pull conventional; it's only the best if you can get into position for it.
He tried sumo deadlift for eight months to a year, it never felt right, so he dropped it and went back to conventional and snatch-grip deadlifts, which feel amazing.
Joint pain is never worth it: it never goes away, only piles up and worsens until it stops you from training at all.

exercises.why: good alternative for people who can't pull conventional; but it never felt right for him after 8-12 months

exercises.why: agree with more people than the bench press
